Row 1 of each sheet is a caption and row 3 holds the headers (pandas: read_excel(..., sheet_name=None, header=2)).
Each row's case and solve: the Case, Solved at and Results columns.
Export fixture: a tee, a PRV, a demand, a strainer and a cooler, with two scenarios.
Units: heads, grade lines, losses and NPSH
Units: fractions (speed, efficiency, flow ÷ rated flow)
Pressures are gauge unless marked (a) or psia; differences carry no marker.

The trace, the methods text, the server's flag messages and the JSON columns are in SI as the server reported them. The app's sentences (flag messages, the goal seek report) give speeds and efficiencies in % and powers in kW (hp with gpm). A Cv (US gpm of water at 1 psi) or Kv (m³/h of water at 1 bar) is as entered in every unit system.
Fractions (speed, efficiency) are 0–1 and carry no unit. Flow ÷ rated flow is a signed ratio with no unit: 1 at the rated flow, negative when the flow runs from outlet to inlet.

Full precision: each number is the value the calculation server returned, converted to these units, not rounded. The app shows 4 significant figures, and heads, elevations and lengths to at least 0.01 m (or its equivalent); it shows head differences below 1×10⁻⁷ m, valve and equipment pressure drops and equipment pressure losses below ρg·10⁻⁷ m and branch K below 1×10⁻⁴ as ≈ 0 (round-off). The file gives them as computed. Spreadsheets display and re-save at most 15 significant digits.

+ inlet → outlet; flow ÷ rated flow, the pressure loss and the head loss are signed like it; the static pressure drop, inlet minus outlet, also holds the ports' elevation and velocity terms, so its sign need not follow the flow.
Losses are signed like the flow: negative where the flow runs to → from (outlet → inlet for valves); a branch path's loss is positive in the flow direction.
Elevations and heads are measured from the project datum.

Methods — Plant water header — all cases (each row's case and solve: Case, Solved at, Results) — SI base units — SI, as reported

- Global Gradient Algorithm (Todini & Pilati 1988): Newton's method on the energy grade line at every node and the flow in every link; sparse direct solve of the Schur complement (SciPy SuperLU, splu). One solver for every topology; every connected part needs a reservoir or reference node.

- Converged when the largest flow change is at most the project tolerance times the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s), continuity closes at every node and over every component to 1e-09 x the largest flow + 1e-14 m³/s, and the energy equation holds on every link to 1e-07 m. On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

- An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
- This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
- This solve: 10 Newton iterations in 2 outer iteration(s); converged.

- Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

- Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

- Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
- Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

- A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).

- Assigned-flow nodes fix the flow leaving the network at their port (a demand, positive) or entering it (a supply, negative), whatever the pressure there: a nodal demand in the continuity equations, as EPANET's junction demands; their pressure is a result. They are not a fixed-pressure boundary. A dead-end branch to one carries its flow. A part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements carries assigned flows only if they sum to zero (to the continuity tolerance): its flows are then solved and its pressure level is not (flagged); otherwise the closed elements around that part whose status rules open as its pressure falls (a net demand) or rises (a net supply) are re-opened; with none left to open, no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the nodes and the elements closed around them (EPANET: a disconnected system). A flow control (an FCV, or a speed-controlled pump) that alone feeds assigned-flow nodes taking its setpoint flow leaves the pressure between them undetermined (reported as not converged, naming them); with another flow the node's flow passes and the control's rules take it to a limit (an FCV fully open below its setpoint, a speed-controlled pump at its maximum or minimum speed), or, above what the control can pass, or with reverse flow through it, no steady state carries it.
- Todini, E., and S. Pilati. A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks. Computer Applications in Water Supply, Vol. 1. Wiley, 1988, 1-20.
- Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
- Darcy–Weisbach head loss h = f (L/D) v²/(2g), g = 9.80665 m/s² (standard gravity, fluids.constants.g), Re = |v| D/ν.
- Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
- Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

- Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

- Pipe dimensions: ASME B36.10M / B36.19M and ASTM D1785 via fluids.piping; roughness: Farshad & Rieke (2006) via fluids.friction.roughness_Farshad; user values where entered (each element's trace names its sources).
- Swamee, P. K., and A. K. Jain. J. Hydraulics Div. ASCE 102(5), 1976, 657-664.
- Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
- Fitting loss h = n K v²/(2g), K from the cited fluids correlation for the fitting type (data/fittings.json) at the reference pipe's inner diameter; a user K overrides it.
- Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.
- Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
- Rennels, D. C., and H. M. Hudson. Pipe Flow: A Practical and Comprehensive Guide. Wiley, 2012.
- Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

- lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

- A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

- Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

- Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

- A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
- Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
- Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.

- Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
- Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
- No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
- Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

- System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which. With assigned-flow nodes, the cut counts their flows as fixed demands and supplies (Gale): a demand on the pump's side of the cut takes part of the forced flow, and one beyond it adds to what the cut must pass. Read the other way, the cut bounds the flow from below: a flowing point below the least flow that assigned flows need through the pump (a demand on its discharge side that a one-way element keeps every reservoir and reference node from feeding, or a supply on its suction side that one keeps from draining) has no steady state either and is not solved again, and one at that floor is solved with each FCV of the cut held open too. A side of the pump that reaches only assigned-flow nodes has no point with a head.
- Fritsch, F. N., and R. E. Carlson. Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17(2), 1980, 238-246.

- Fritsch, F. N., and J. Butland. A method for constructing local monotone piecewise cubic interpolants. SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 5(2), 1984, 300-304, doi:10.1137/0905021 (the derivative formula of scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator).
- Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).

- Ford, L. R., and D. R. Fulkerson. Maximal flow through a network. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 8, 1956, 399-404 (the max-flow min-cut theorem: the flows no state carries through a pump on its system curve).

- Gale, D. A theorem on flows in networks. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 7(2), 1957, 1073-1082 (a flow with fixed supplies and demands exists when no node set holds more net supply than its cut can pass: the assigned flows in a pump's system-curve bounds).

- Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

- Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

- PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
- Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

- An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

- A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).

- System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which. With assigned-flow nodes, the cut counts their flows as fixed demands and supplies (Gale): a demand on the pump's side of the cut takes part of the forced flow, and one beyond it adds to what the cut must pass. Read the other way, the cut bounds the flow from below: a flowing point below the least flow that assigned flows need through the pump (a demand on its discharge side that a one-way element keeps every reservoir and reference node from feeding, or a supply on its suction side that one keeps from draining) has no steady state either and is not solved again, and one at that floor is solved with each FCV of the cut held open too. A side of the pump that reaches only assigned-flow nodes has no point with a head.

On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

- An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
- This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
- This solve: 10 Newton iterations in 2 outer iteration(s); converged.

- Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

- Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

- Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
- Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

- A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).

- Assigned-flow nodes fix the flow leaving the network at their port (a demand, positive) or entering it (a supply, negative), whatever the pressure there: a nodal demand in the continuity equations, as EPANET's junction demands; their pressure is a result. They are not a fixed-pressure boundary. A dead-end branch to one carries its flow. A part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements carries assigned flows only if they sum to zero (to the continuity tolerance): its flows are then solved and its pressure level is not (flagged); otherwise the closed elements around that part whose status rules open as its pressure falls (a net demand) or rises (a net supply) are re-opened; with none left to open, no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the nodes and the elements closed around them (EPANET: a disconnected system). A flow control (an FCV, or a speed-controlled pump) that alone feeds assigned-flow nodes taking its setpoint flow leaves the pressure between them undetermined (reported as not converged, naming them); with another flow the node's flow passes and the control's rules take it to a limit (an FCV fully open below its setpoint, a speed-controlled pump at its maximum or minimum speed), or, above what the control can pass, or with reverse flow through it, no steady state carries it.

- Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
- Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

- Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

- Fitting loss h = n K v²/(2g), K from the cited fluids correlation for the fitting type (data/fittings.json) at the reference pipe's inner diameter; a user K overrides it.
- Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.
- Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
- Rennels, D. C., and H. M. Hudson. Pipe Flow: A Practical and Comprehensive Guide. Wiley, 2012.
- Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

- lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

- A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

- Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

- Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

- A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
- Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
- Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.

- Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
- Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
- No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
- Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

- System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which. With assigned-flow nodes, the cut counts their flows as fixed demands and supplies (Gale): a demand on the pump's side of the cut takes part of the forced flow, and one beyond it adds to what the cut must pass. Read the other way, the cut bounds the flow from below: a flowing point below the least flow that assigned flows need through the pump (a demand on its discharge side that a one-way element keeps every reservoir and reference node from feeding, or a supply on its suction side that one keeps from draining) has no steady state either and is not solved again, and one at that floor is solved with each FCV of the cut held open too. A side of the pump that reaches only assigned-flow nodes has no point with a head.

- Gale, D. A theorem on flows in networks. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 7(2), 1957, 1073-1082 (a flow with fixed supplies and demands exists when no node set holds more net supply than its cut can pass: the assigned flows in a pump's system-curve bounds).

- Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

- Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

- PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
- Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

- An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

- A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).

- ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
- Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.

- Equipment (one side of a heat exchanger, a coil, a strainer, a filter, or another passive element given by its datasheet): the loss of total head from its inlet to its outlet is h = EGL_in − EGL_out = c Q|Q| (a loss of total pressure ρ g h), with c = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g Q_r²) from the rated pressure drop ΔP_r at the rated flow Q_r for a fluid of density ρ_r: a constant K, the square law of ISA-75.01.01-2007 eq. (1) for non-choked, turbulent liquid flow, and the high-Re limit of the 3-K method (Silverberg & Darby). The rated drop is the dissipative loss (friction and form) of total pressure between the ports, without the static head between them: each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in its connected pipe, so the static drop reported is ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2.

- Density scaling: the pressure loss at the solved flow is ρ g h = ΔP_r (ρ/ρ_r)(Q/Q_r)², with ρ the fluid being solved. The operating density cancels out of the head loss h, which the rating alone sets; it only converts head to pressure.

- A Cv or Kv rating is a rated point on water by definition (1 psi at Cv US gpm, 1 bar at Kv m³/h): c = K/(2 g A²) with K from fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01-2007, water at 999.29744568 kg/m³), the valves' conversion, evaluated at a 1 m bore; K ∝ D⁴ makes K/A² the same on every bore, so no pipe diameter is needed. Its pressure loss is (ρ/ρ_w) × 1 psi × (Q/Cv gpm)², or × 1 bar × (Q/Kv m³/h)².
- Reverse flow (outlet → inlet) follows the same, symmetric law and is flagged: no datasheet rates reverse flow.
- Laminar flow (Re < 2000) in the end segment of a connected pipe is flagged, as for a valve's Cv or Kv: the square law is the turbulent-flow law, and the loss is then likely underestimated.

- At zero flow the law's slope 2c|Q| is 0: Newton's Jacobian uses at least 1e-06 x the slopes of the pipes at the element's ports there, as for every link that is not a pipe (EPANET 2.2 bounds such a gradient instead); the law itself is exact.

- Viscosity is not corrected: the loss scales with density only. With a fluid more viscous than the rating's, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives (a smooth-tube element dominated by friction scales as ρ^0.75 μ^0.25 Q^1.75 by Blasius' law); a correction needs the equipment's geometry or its vendor's own factors.

- Every port's absolute static pressure is checked against the vapor pressure (0 Pa absolute when none is known) and flagged where the liquid would flash.

- The energy grade line EGL = z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) is the nodal unknown; the hydraulic grade line HGL = EGL − v²/(2g), with v the velocity in the pipe connected at the port. Pump head is the EGL rise.
- Flow is positive from a connection's 'from' port to its 'to' port; branch port flows are positive into the component.
- Every element's trace lists its inputs (with their source: user, default, library or computed), equations, correlations, data sources and intermediate values.
- Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
- Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

- No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one (removable), and none at a reference node; each boundary's trace lists the entrance and exit fittings at its ports.
- Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
- Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
- Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
- Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
- Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.
- Equipment losses scale with the square of the flow and with density from one rated point, a Cv or a Kv (constant K); viscosity is not corrected.
